title: Cybersecurity: secure what you own, then learn to spot and handle trouble
intro: Security is risk reduction, not perfection. Fix the cheap, common problems first, watch the logs, and have a plan for the day something goes wrong. Everything here is defensive and runs against your own app or public sites.
outcome: A clean self-audit, one log investigation written up as an incident, and a short playbook you could follow under stress.

steps.title: Audit your own setup
steps.what: Most breaches start with a leaked key or an open door you forgot about.
how: Open the Self-audit tab and run it.
Fix every red item: .env in .gitignore, no secrets in tracked files, tight CORS.
Run it again and note the score.
steps.done_when: Score is up and no red item is left unexplained.
mistakes: Fixing nothing because 'it is only personal'.
Committing a key, then deleting it (it stays in history; rotate it).
steps.ask: Which self-audit failures matter most for me?

steps.title: Read the logs for patterns
how: Open the Logs tab and load the sample.
Read each detection and the lines behind it.
Decide for each: attack, noise or a mistake by a real user.
steps.done_when: You can explain one detection and the evidence for it.
mistakes: Treating a detection as proof.
Ignoring a success after many failures from the same address.
steps.ask: Explain this brute-force detection and what I should check.

steps.title: Check what a site shows the world
steps.what: Headers and certificates are the cheapest protections.
how: Open Web checks and enter a public site you own.
Read the missing headers and what each one prevents.
Note the certificate expiry date.
steps.done_when: You have a list of missing headers ranked by importance.
mistakes: Testing sites you don't own.
steps.ask: Which missing header should I add first?

steps.title: Know what your machine exposes
steps.what: A service you forgot about is an open door.
how: Open Ports and run the local check.
For each open port, name the program and why it is needed.
Close or firewall the rest.
steps.done_when: Every open port has a reason.
mistakes: Assuming a database port is only reachable locally.
steps.ask: What does an open port 5432 mean?

steps.title: Understand hashes, passwords and 2FA
steps.what: Never store passwords; store salted slow hashes. Add a second factor.
how: Hash a word in the Crypto tab and change one letter.
Test a few passwords for strength and read the assumption behind the crack time.
Set up the TOTP lab and match the code.
steps.done_when: You can say why a hash is not encryption.
mistakes: Believing a long common phrase is strong.
Using SHA-256 alone for passwords.
steps.ask: Why are fast hashes bad for passwords?

steps.title: Handle an incident on paper
steps.what: In a real incident you won't think clearly; the checklist thinks for you.
how: Open Incidents and log one from the sample log.
Work through the playbook checklist for its category.
Close it with a note on what you would change.
steps.done_when: A closed incident with lessons learned.
mistakes: Deleting evidence while cleaning up.
No written timeline.
steps.ask: Walk me through the first hour of a suspected key leak.

steps.title: Read honeypot logs like an analyst
steps.what: A honeypot is a decoy that records what attackers try. The skill is turning thousands of log lines into a short list of what to block and what to alert on.
how: Open Honeypot logs, load the sample and read the counts: usernames, passwords, source IPs.
Look at the command classes. Say which command in the sample is recon, which downloads and which executes.
Notice the URL is shown defanged. Say why you never click or fetch it.
Read the slips: which files Cowrie really writes, and why 'real attacks' and 'isolated lab' cannot both be true.
Write two rules for your own servers from what the bots tried (for example, disable password SSH, alert on new cron entries).
steps.done_when: You can name three things a honeypot log teaches you and one you must never do with its downloads.
mistakes: Running or opening a file the attacker uploaded.
Exposing a honeypot on the network you use for real work.
Treating your own test traffic as attacker statistics.
steps.ask: What would you change on a real SSH server after reading this log?

steps.title: Harden a Windows endpoint, one measured change at a time
steps.what: Most breaches use basic gaps: old protocols, exposed remote access, too many admins and missed patches. Hardening is finding those gaps on a machine and closing them safely.
how: Open Endpoint hardening. Copy the read-only script, read it line by line to confirm it only reads settings, then run it in PowerShell on a PC you own.
Paste the output and grade it. Sort the failures by severity.
Pick the top failure and write the change, the test and the backout plan before touching anything.
Make the change on one machine, re-run the script and confirm the line turned to pass.
Read the slips in the source guide: which claims are unsourced or out of date, and what the guide leaves out (MFA, encryption, backups, LAPS).
steps.done_when: You can name three failing checks, the risk behind each and how you would roll one out safely.
mistakes: Turning off SMB1 or NTLM everywhere at once without auditing what still needs it.
Treating a passing score as proof the PC is secure.
Running a script from the internet without reading it first.
steps.ask: Which hardening failure on my report should I fix first, and how do I test it?

steps.title: Judge a design against the five principles and the CIA triad
steps.what: Most security failures are design failures: one layer carrying everything, too much access, one person controlling a process. Five principles (defense in depth, least privilege, separation of duties, security by design, KISS) and one anti-pattern (security by obscurity) give you questions to ask about any system.
how: Open Cybersecurity > Principles and NIST CSF > The principles and read the red flag and the question for each one.
Open Principles check, load the sample and read which principle each finding breaks and the fix.
Write two sentences about a setup you know (your home network, a workplace app) and run them through the check.
Open CIA classifier, load the sample incident and say which of confidentiality, integrity and availability it hit, and which control would have helped.
Ask the three CIA questions of a project: what was read, what was changed, what stopped working?
steps.done_when: You can name the principle a given weakness breaks, and match an attack to the property it hits and one control that counters it.
mistakes: Treating security by obscurity as a sixth principle. It is the anti-pattern: a hidden URL or a secret algorithm is not access control.
Thinking a keyword check replaces a review. It only points at wording.
Putting every control at the perimeter and calling it depth.
steps.ask: Here is how our small office is set up. Which of the five principles does it break and what would I change first?

steps.title: Run a NIST Cybersecurity Framework self-check
steps.what: The NIST CSF organises a security programme into functions: Govern (added in CSF 2.0), Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. They are not steps in order; they run together. A self-check shows where you are thin.
how: Open Principles and NIST CSF > NIST CSF self-check.
Answer yes, partly or no for each question honestly, for a real place (home lab, small business, your employer if allowed).
Score it and read the weakest function first.
Take the top three 'do these next' items and write an owner and a date for each.
Repeat in three months and compare. Notice which function moved.
steps.done_when: You can name the six functions, say which one an action belongs to (an incident plan is Respond, a restore test is Recover) and explain why they are a cycle, not a sequence.
mistakes: Answering yes because a policy exists on paper and nobody follows it.
Fixing the strongest function because it is easiest.
Reading the score as an audit result.
steps.ask: My scores are low on Detect and Recover. What are the cheapest first steps for a five-person business?
